units.signature: fn arith_ok(op: int, a: int, b: int) -> [] bool
units.description: Whether applying the binary operation op to a and b is allowed: it neither traps nor falls outside the signed 64-bit range -9223372036854775808..9223372036854775807. op is a code: 0 is a + b, 1 is a - b, 2 is a * b, 3 is a / b, 4 is a % b. True exactly when the mathematically exact result fits in that range and, for 3 and 4, b is not 0. So 9223372036854775807 + 1 is false, -9223372036854775807 - 2 is false, minimum * -1 is false, minimum / -1 is false, but minimum % -1 is true (that remainder is 0). It must itself never trap, for any a and b: cancho's own + - * trap on overflow, so test against the limits first or use wrapping_mul and a division to check a product. The minimum cannot be written as a literal (9223372036854775808 does not parse); write -9223372036854775807 - 1.
tests: fn ok_is(op: int, a: int, b: int, want: bool) -> [] int { if arith_ok(op, a, b) == want { return 0; } return 1; }

pub fn test_arith_sub_edges() -> [] int { test.assert_eq(ok_is(1, 0, 9223372036854775807, true), 0); test.assert_eq(ok_is(1, -2, 9223372036854775807, false), 0); test.assert_eq(ok_is(1, 0, -9223372036854775807 - 1, false), 0); test.assert_eq(ok_is(1, -1, -9223372036854775807 - 1, true), 0); return 0; }

pub fn test_arith_mul_edges() -> [] int { test.assert_eq(ok_is(2, 3037000499, 3037000499, true), 0); test.assert_eq(ok_is(2, 3037000500, 3037000500, false), 0); test.assert_eq(ok_is(2, -9223372036854775807 - 1, -1, false), 0); test.assert_eq(ok_is(2, -1, -9223372036854775807 - 1, false), 0); test.assert_eq(ok_is(2, -9223372036854775807 - 1, 1, true), 0); test.assert_eq(ok_is(2, 0, -9223372036854775807 - 1, true), 0); return 0; }

pub fn test_arith_div_rem_edges() -> [] int { test.assert_eq(ok_is(3, -9223372036854775807 - 1, -1, false), 0); test.assert_eq(ok_is(3, -9223372036854775807 - 1, 1, true), 0); test.assert_eq(ok_is(4, -9223372036854775807 - 1, -1, true), 0); test.assert_eq(ok_is(4, 5, 0, false), 0); test.assert_eq(ok_is(3, 0, 0, false), 0); return 0; }

units.signature: fn arith_apply(op: int, a: int, b: int) -> [] int
units.description: The result of the operation op on a and b, with the same op codes as arith_ok (0 +, 1 -, 2 *, 3 /, 4 %). It may assume arith_ok(op, a, b) is true and need not check. Division truncates toward zero, as in C: 7 / 2 is 3, -7 / 2 is -3, 7 / -2 is -3; the remainder takes the sign of the dividend: -7 % 2 is -1, 7 % -2 is 1.
The index of the first byte at or after pos that is not an ASCII space (0x20), or len(s) if there is none. Only the space counts: a tab or a newline is not skipped. pos is between 0 and len(s).

Reads a decimal number starting at st[0]. The state st is a slice of two ints that every parsing function shares: st[0] is the current position in s and st[1] is the error flag (0 means fine; anything else means an error was found, and it is never cleared). Reads the maximal run of ASCII digits 0-9 at st[0] (leading zeros allowed; spaces are NOT skipped here), sets st[0] to the index just after the last digit and returns the value. If there is no digit at st[0] (including st[0] >= len(s)), sets st[1] = 1. If the value would exceed 9223372036854775807, sets st[1] = 1; it must not trap while detecting this (compare against the limit before multiplying by 10). On error the returned value and st[0] are unspecified. It does not change st[1] otherwise, and never reads past the end of s. In the examples `st` stands for a fresh state [0, 0] (an example cannot build a slice; the unit's tests do).
tests: fn num_ok(s: &static [byte], pos: int, want: int, want_pos: int) -> [] int { var bad = 1; region a { let st = alloc_slice[a](2, 0); st[0] = pos; let v = read_number(s, st); if st[1] == 0 && v == want && st[0] == want_pos { bad = 0; } } return bad; }
fn num_bad(s: &static [byte], pos: int) -> [] int { var bad = 1; region a { let st = alloc_slice[a](2, 0); st[0] = pos; read_number(s, st); if st[1] != 0 { bad = 0; } } return bad; }
pub fn test_num_ok_1() -> [] int { test.assert_eq(num_ok("12", 0, 12, 2), 0); return 0; }

units.signature: fn parse_level[&r, &q](s: &r [byte], st: &!q [int], level: int) -> [] int
units.description: The recursive core: parses and evaluates one grammar level of the expression starting at st[0], with the same two-int state as read_number (st[0] position, st[1] error flag, 0 = fine). level 0 is a sum: a level-1 operand followed by any number of (+ or -) level-1 operands, applied left to right. level 1 is a product: a level-2 operand followed by any number of (*, / or %) level-2 operands, applied left to right. level 2 is an atom: after skipping spaces it is either a '-' followed by a level-2 atom (unary minus, so '--3' works), or a '(' followed by a level-0 expression and then a ')', or a number (read_number). Spaces are skipped before every token (never inside a number). Every binary operation is checked with arith_ok before arith_apply, and a unary minus is checked as arith_ok(1, 0, v). Any failure (unexpected end of text, missing ')', a failed arith_ok, division by zero, overflow) sets st[1] = 1; once st[1] is nonzero every level stops and returns 0 without reading further, so it always terminates. A byte that is not a token for the loop (a letter, a tab, ')', ...) simply ends the loops at levels 0 and 1; the caller decides whether leftovers are an error. On success st[0] is the index just after the last byte of the last token consumed (trailing spaces are not consumed). On error the value and st[0] are unspecified. Level 0 parses a whole expression; the recursion goes level 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> (parenthesis) -> 0 and must survive 10000 nested parentheses. cancho allows a function to call itself (use level + 1 for the next level). In the examples `st` stands for a fresh state [0, 0] (an example cannot build a slice; the unit's tests do).
tests: fn lvl_ok(s: &static [byte], level: int, want: int, want_pos: int) -> [] int { var bad = 1; region a { let st = alloc_slice[a](2, 0); let v = parse_level(s, st, level); if st[1] == 0 && v == want && st[0] == want_pos { bad = 0; } } return bad; }
fn lvl_bad(s: &static [byte], level: int) -> [] int { var bad = 1; region a { let st = alloc_slice[a](2, 0); parse_level(s, st, level); if st[1] != 0 { bad = 0; } } return bad; }

units.description: Evaluate the whole text: Ok(value), or Err(message) (any message) when the text is not exactly one valid expression, or a step overflows, or divides by zero. Make the two-int state (region + alloc_slice[a](2, 0), starting [0, 0]), call parse_level(s, st, 0), then skip trailing spaces: anything left (a stray ')', a second number, a letter, a tab, a newline) is an error, and so is an empty text, and so is st[1] != 0. The language: numbers of ASCII digits, + - * / % with * / % tighter than + -, left associative, unary minus (repeatable; no unary plus), parentheses, ASCII spaces between tokens and at the ends. Arithmetic is exact signed 64-bit; every intermediate result (each operation, each unary minus, each literal) must fit -9223372036854775808..9223372036854775807 or the answer is Err, so '9223372036854775807+1-1' is Err. Division and remainder truncate toward zero (C). Division or remainder by zero is Err; minimum / -1 is Err but minimum % -1 is 0. The minimum can only be written -9223372036854775807-1; the literal 9223372036854775808 is Err. It must never trap, on any bytes. The Result is std.result's: result.Result::Ok(v), result.Result::Err("...").
tests: fn ev_is(s: &static [byte], want: int) -> [] int { match expr_eval(s) { result.Result::Ok(v) => { if v == want { return 0; } return 1; } result.Result::Err(_) => { return 2; } } }
fn ev_err(s: &static [byte]) -> [] int { match expr_eval(s) { result.Result::Ok(_) => { return 1; } result.Result::Err(_) => { return 0; } } }
